title: Stri: Gandhari's curse
hook: a grieving mother turns to Krishna and curses him, and he answers with something close to a smile
carry: he takes it without striking back

segments.voice: Yesterday in Stri, Gandhari was given sight and turned it on the women searching the field. Your line was look at this, she says. Did you notice who was left cleaning up after a fight? Today, the curse. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

She has been talking to Krishna the whole time. Look at this widow, look at that mother, look at my son. And somewhere in that long walk across the field, the grief turns. Gandhari stops describing and starts accusing. You could have stopped this, she says to him. You had the power. You had the words. Both sides listened to you, and you let it happen. This is the curse in our title, and it isn't aimed at the Pandavas. It's aimed at Krishna himself, standing right next to her. Today, what Gandhari says, and how Krishna takes it.
screen: `THE GRIEF TURNS.` → `"YOU COULD HAVE STOPPED THIS."` → `THE CURSE IS FOR KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: Gandhari reaches for the power her discipline has given her, the power she held back with Yudhishthira. Because you stood by while the Kurus and the Pandavas destroyed each other, she says, your own people will destroy each other. Your kinsmen, the Vrishnis, will kill one another. You yourself will die alone, in a wild place, by an inglorious means. And the women of your house will weep over their dead, the way the women of my house are weeping now. She has just spent this book looking at grieving women. Now she wishes that same scene on Krishna's family. Then the surprise. Krishna doesn't argue. He doesn't defend himself or explain the war. In Ganguli's telling he answers with a kind of calm, almost a smile. I already knew this, he says, in effect. My people can't be destroyed by anyone else, and they will destroy themselves. You've only spoken what was going to happen. And then he turns her own grief back to her, gently. The war came, he says, from your son's choices, and from your own failure to restrain him. Get up. Don't give yourself to sorrow. Gandhari falls silent. So the curse lands, and Krishna accepts it. The book doesn't settle whether she was right to blame him. It lets a mother say something almost unsayable to Krishna, whom the epic honors as God, and lets him take it without striking back. The epic will come back to this curse. For now, it simply hangs in the air over the field.
screen: `SHE CURSES KRISHNA'S PEOPLE` · `HE ANSWERS CALMLY` · `"I ALREADY KNEW"` · then, large: `THE CURSE IS ACCEPTED`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, hands open on your knees. Bring to mind a question you've wanted to shout at life, or at God, or at whoever was in charge when something went wrong. You don't need to answer it. Breathe in, and let the question be as loud as it really is. Breathe out, and notice that it can be said and the world still holds. If you pray, you can bring that question into your prayer just as it is. The bell holds the time.
Stri. Woman. The book where a mother's grief becomes a curse on Krishna, and he accepts it.

Your line: he takes it without striking back. Today, when someone's grief comes out as blame, let it land without striking back. Tomorrow, the water offered for the dead, and a secret. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Gandhari's curse on Krishna is told in temple discourses, plays and retellings of the epic, and storytellers link it to the later end of Krishna's own clan.

she cursed Krishna, for not stopping the war.

fork.setup: you're Krishna. a grieving mother has just cursed your whole family for a war you didn't stop. what do you do?
options: explain why the war had to happen.
accept it calmly, and say you already knew.
fork.reveal: Krishna answers with a kind of calm, says only he could bring his people's end, and then gently tells her to rise from her grief.

original.note: curse: a word spoken with the power of a person's discipline, which in the epics comes true.

trapdoor: what you thought: Gandhari's curse is about the Pandavas.
what it means: she curses Krishna, and his clan, for letting the war happen.
what a scholar hears: God is blamed by a grieving mother and accepts it, and the curse becomes the seed of the epic's later book about the end of Krishna's clan.

notes: All paraphrase. Gandhari's curse in Ganguli names a specific number of years before it falls; the number is left out under the claims rule. A Keeper may want it restored.

Confirm Krishna's reply: that he knew, that the Vrishnis can be destroyed by none but themselves (or himself), and that he tells Gandhari the war came from her son's wickedness and her own fault, then bids her rise. 'Almost a smile' paraphrases the text's description; confirm.
Theological framing 'something almost unsayable to God': check it is acceptable to Vaishnava readers.
Editor: cut the stock line 'a deeply human moment'; 'the whole book' softened; the hook now names Krishna rather than the narrator calling him God.

Audit: Ganguli has Krishna perish 'by disgusting means' in the wilderness; 'ordinary means' (which understated the curse) changed to 'an inglorious means'. Narrator no longer calls Krishna 'the god' in its own voice; now 'whom the epic honors as God'.
